title: Process states, ps, sessions, daemons, zombies

lessons.title: Process states: R, S, D, T, Z
lessons.goal:
Learn the states a process can be in, how `ps` shows them, and what each state tells you.

Why it matters: "the server is slow" often means many processes in `R` (CPU) or `D` (waiting for disk/network). The state is the first clue.

setup.note: Programs are small C files (gcc needed). PIDs differ on your machine.

steps.title: The states
steps.text:
`ps` shows the state in the `STAT` column.

- **R** running or ready to run (on a CPU or in the run queue)
- **S** sleeping, can be woken by a signal (waiting for input, a timer, a lock)
- **D** uninterruptible sleep (waiting for I/O; cannot be killed until it returns)
- **T** stopped (by a signal such as Ctrl-Z)
- **Z** zombie (finished, waiting for the parent to collect its exit code)
- **I** idle kernel thread

steps.title: S: sleeping
steps.text: Most processes sleep most of the time. `sleep` waits for a timer. `wchan` shows the kernel function it waits in.

run.output:
[1] 3463191
    PID STAT WCHAN                  COMMAND
3463191 S    hrtimer_nanosleep      sleep

steps.title: R: running
steps.text: A busy loop never waits, so it stays `R`. We start one in the background, look at it, and stop it.

run.cmd: sh -c 'while :; do :; done' & echo $! > busy.pid; sleep 1; ps -o pid,stat,pcpu,comm -p $(cat busy.pid)

steps.title: T: stopped
steps.text: `SIGSTOP` freezes a process. It keeps its memory but gets no CPU. `SIGCONT` resumes it.

run.cmd: kill -STOP $(cat busy.pid); sleep 0.5; ps -o stat,comm -p $(cat busy.pid)
kill -CONT $(cat busy.pid); sleep 0.5; ps -o stat,comm -p $(cat busy.pid); kill $(cat busy.pid)

steps.title: The state in /proc
steps.text: `ps` reads `/proc/PID/status`. The same information is there with the full name.

steps.title: D: uninterruptible sleep
steps.text:
A process in `D` waits for hardware or a network file system and **ignores all signals, even SIGKILL**, until the I/O finishes. It counts toward the load average without using CPU. Typical causes: a hung NFS server, a failing disk, a stuck storage driver.

We cannot safely create one here.

run.reason: a D-state hang needs a failing disk or dead NFS server; not reproducible safely on this machine

steps.under: A process in `S` can be woken by a signal and the kernel can abort the wait. In `D` the kernel code is in the middle of an operation that must complete (a disk transfer that writes into memory). Aborting it could corrupt data, so signals wait. Since Linux 2.6.25 some waits use `TASK_KILLABLE`, which fatal signals can interrupt.

quiz.q: Which state counts toward load average but uses no CPU?
quiz.explain: Processes in uninterruptible sleep (D) are counted.

quiz.q: A process in state D ignores which signal?
options: SIGKILL too, until the I/O completes
quiz.explain: That is what makes D-state hangs painful.
Waiting for a timer: interruptible sleep.

check.scenario: `top` shows load average 40 and the CPU is 95% idle. Which process state do you look for and with which command?
check.answer: Many processes in `D` (waiting for I/O). `ps -eo pid,stat,wchan:30,comm | awk '$2 ~ /^D/'` lists them. The `wchan` tells which kernel function they wait in (often a filesystem or block layer function), which points to the stuck disk or NFS mount.

lessons.title: Sessions, process groups and daemons
lessons.goal:
Learn how the kernel groups processes (process group, session), what a controlling terminal is, and how a classic daemon detaches from it.

Why it matters: this explains why background jobs die when you close a terminal, what `nohup` and `setsid` do, and what `systemd` does for you today.

setup.note: Programs are small C files (gcc needed). PIDs differ on your machine.

steps.title: Process groups and sessions
steps.text: Commands in one pipeline form a **process group** (PGID). Here a subshell starts a two-command pipeline; the two `sleep` processes are its children and share one group. (`set -m` turns on job control, which an interactive shell already has: it puts each job in its own group.) Groups that belong to one login belong to a **session** (SID) with a **controlling terminal** (TTY). The terminal sends signals to the foreground group (Ctrl-C = SIGINT).

run.cmd: set -m; (sleep 40 | sleep 41) & sleep 0.5; ps -o pid,ppid,pgid,sid,tty,comm -p $!,$(pgrep -P $! -d,); kill $(pgrep -P $!); set +m

steps.title: setsid: leave the session
steps.text: `setsid CMD` starts CMD in a **new session** with no controlling terminal. Its SID is its own PID and TTY shows `?`.

run.cmd: setsid sleep 42 & sleep 0.5; p=$(pgrep -n -x sleep); ps -o pid,ppid,pgid,sid,tty,comm -p $p; kill $p
run.output:
[1] 3463224
    PID    PPID    PGID     SID TT       COMMAND
3463224 3463212 3463224 3463224 ?        sleep

steps.title: What happens when the terminal closes
steps.text: When a terminal closes, the kernel sends **SIGHUP** to the session leader's foreground group. Most programs die. `nohup` makes the command ignore SIGHUP. We check the signal mask: bit 1 of `SigIgn` is SIGHUP.

run.cmd: nohup sleep 43 > /dev/null 2>&1 & p1=$!; sleep 44 & p2=$!; sleep 0.5; grep SigIgn /proc/$p1/status /proc/$p2/status | sed 's#/proc/[0-9]*/status#process#'; kill $p1 $p2

steps.after: `SigIgn` is a bit mask: the rightmost bit is SIGHUP (1), the next SIGINT (2), then SIGQUIT (3). The shell itself makes background jobs ignore SIGINT and SIGQUIT, so the plain process shows `6`. Only the nohup process also has the SIGHUP bit, so it shows `7`.

steps.title: A classic daemon, written by hand
steps.text: A **daemon** is a background service without a terminal. The traditional recipe: fork and let the parent exit (so the child is adopted by PID 1), `setsid` to get a new session, fork again so it can never regain a terminal, change to `/`, and point stdin/out/err at `/dev/null`.

run.output:
PID    PPID    PGID     SID TT       COMMAND
3463291 1373549 3463290 3463290 ?        daemonize

steps.after: TTY is `?`: no controlling terminal. SID and PGID are the PID of the first child, which has already exited, so the daemon itself is **not** a session leader and can never open a controlling terminal. Its PPID is not our shell any more: it was adopted by an init-like process (PID 1, or a per-user `systemd --user` that acts as subreaper).

steps.title: Clean up and the modern way
steps.text: We stop the daemon. Today you do not write this code: you write a **systemd unit** and systemd starts the process in the background, gives it logging and restarts it (module 25).

run.cmd: pkill -x daemonize; sleep 0.5; pgrep -x daemonize || echo 'daemon stopped'

steps.under: The double fork is not needed under systemd: the service manager already runs the process without a terminal in its own session and cgroup (`Type=simple`). Old-style daemons that fork need `Type=forking` so systemd can track the final PID.

options: Sets the session ID to a number
Runs a command in a new session without a controlling terminal
quiz.explain: New session, new process group, no TTY.

quiz.q: Which signal does the kernel send to a session when its terminal closes?
Why does a classic daemon fork twice?
options: So it can never acquire a controlling terminal again
quiz.explain: A session leader can open a terminal and get it as controlling terminal; the second child is not a session leader.

quiz.q: What does the TTY column show for a daemon?

check.scenario: You start a long job over SSH and the connection drops; the job is gone. List three ways to keep it alive.
check.answer: `nohup CMD &` (ignores SIGHUP and logs to nohup.out), `setsid CMD &` (no controlling terminal, so no SIGHUP), or a terminal multiplexer such as `tmux` or `screen`. For services use a systemd unit or `systemd-run --user`.

lessons.title: Zombies, orphans and reaping
lessons.goal:
Create a zombie and an orphan on purpose, see them in `ps`, and learn who cleans them up.

Why it matters: zombie buildup means a parent forgets to `wait()`. It fills the process table, and `kill -9` cannot help. You must fix or kill the parent.

setup.note: Programs are small C files (gcc needed). PIDs differ on your machine.

steps.title: A parent that never waits
steps.text: When a process ends, the kernel frees its memory but keeps a tiny entry with the exit status until the parent calls `wait`. That entry is a **zombie**. This parent creates a child that exits at once and then sleeps without calling `wait`.

run.output:
[1] 3463311
parent 3463311: child 3463312 has exited, but I never call wait()

steps.title: See the zombie
steps.text: `Z` in STAT and `<defunct>` in the command mark a zombie. It has no memory and no CPU use. It still has a PID.

run.output:
PID    PPID STAT COMMAND
3463312 3463311 Z    zombie <defunct>

steps.title: You cannot kill a zombie
steps.text: It is already dead. A signal has no process to run in. The fix is to make the parent call `wait`, or to remove the parent. Then PID 1 (or a subreaper) adopts the zombie and reaps it at once.

run.cmd: kill -9 $(ps -o pid= --ppid $(pgrep -x zombie)); sleep 0.5; ps -o pid,ppid,stat,comm --ppid $(pgrep -x zombie)
run.output:
PID    PPID STAT COMMAND
3463312 3463311 Z    zombie <defunct>

run.cmd: kill $(pgrep -x zombie); sleep 1; ps -o pid,ppid,stat,comm -C zombie || echo 'both gone'
run.output:
bash: kill: (3463312) - No such process
    PID    PPID STAT COMMAND
both gone

steps.under: The kernel keeps the zombie's `task_struct` so the parent can read the exit status (`wait4`) and resource usage. When the parent exits, its children are re-parented to the nearest **subreaper** or to PID 1, which calls `wait` in a loop. A container's PID 1 that does not do this (a plain app) lets zombies pile up.

steps.title: An orphan is the opposite
steps.text: An **orphan** is a living child whose parent exited. The kernel re-parents it to PID 1 (or a subreaper). It is harmless: it keeps running and is reaped later.

run.output:
parent 3463342 exits first
child: my parent is now 1373549
done

steps.after: The child printed its new parent: an init-like process, not our shell's child. The number shown depends on whether a subreaper (for example `systemd --user`) exists in your session.

options: A process using too much CPU
A finished process whose exit status has not been collected
quiz.explain: Z state: dead but still in the table.

quiz.q: Why does `kill -9` not remove a zombie?
options: It is already dead; only the parent's wait can remove it
quiz.explain: There is no running code to receive the signal.

quiz.q: Who reaps the zombie after its parent exits?
quiz.explain: The orphaned zombie is adopted and waited for.

options: A running child whose parent has exited
quiz.explain: It keeps running under a new parent.

check.scenario: Monitoring shows 5000 zombie processes on a server. How do you find the cause and fix it?
check.answer: `ps -eo pid,ppid,stat,comm | awk '$3 ~ /^Z/'` lists them; count by PPID with `| awk '{print $2}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn` to find the parent that does not call `wait`. Restart or fix that parent (it must handle SIGCHLD and `wait`). Killing the zombies is impossible; restarting the parent lets PID 1 reap them.

interview.q: Name the process states shown by ps.
interview.a: R running/runnable, S interruptible sleep, D uninterruptible sleep, T stopped, Z zombie, I idle kernel thread. See [the lesson](#/lesson/10/process-states).

interview.q: What is a zombie and how do you get rid of it?
interview.a: A finished process whose parent has not called wait. You cannot kill it. Fix the parent so it waits, or restart/kill the parent so PID 1 reaps the zombie. See [zombies](#/lesson/10/zombies-orphans).

interview.q: What is a process in D state?
interview.a: It waits uninterruptibly for I/O. It cannot be killed until the I/O returns. Many D processes raise the load average with idle CPUs.

interview.q: How does a classic daemon detach from the terminal?
interview.a: fork (parent exits), setsid, fork again, chdir to /, redirect stdin/out/err to /dev/null. See [the daemon](#/lesson/10/sessions-daemons).

interview.q: What is the difference between an orphan and a zombie?
interview.a: An orphan is alive and re-parented to PID 1. A zombie is dead and waits for its parent to collect the status.

interview.q: Why can a container's PID 1 cause zombies?
interview.a: PID 1 must reap adopted children. A normal application as PID 1 often does not call wait, so zombies accumulate. Use an init such as tini (`docker run --init`).

glossary.def: A terminated process whose exit status has not been collected by its parent (state Z).
A running process whose parent has exited; it is adopted by PID 1 or a subreaper.
State D: waiting for I/O, ignores signals until it completes.
A set of processes that receive terminal signals together, for example a pipeline.
A set of process groups belonging to one login, tied to a controlling terminal.
A background service process without a controlling terminal.
A process that adopts orphaned descendants instead of PID 1.
